tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — NATIVE TEXAS BROME, CHECK GLUMES
tiles.details: Cleveland Powell's source-labelled Texas-brome photo (panel 0) shows several narrow MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets, projecting awnlike tips and emerging yellow anthers. The published 4–7 florets per spikelet have NOT been counted or measured from these unscaled pixels. The original photo crops out the plant base. New Texas source-verified panel 12 shows a flowering shoot growing in rocky soil, and panels 9–11 show attached flowering branches and green spikelets. Actual fibrous roots are still underground and no one image documents a continuous extracted root-to-head specimen. Panel 1 is a historically printed Hitchcock/Chase LINE DRAWING, not a second plant photograph. FNA describes a loose panicle 8–15 cm long and spikelets about 20–30 mm with 4–7 florets, but the photograph has no scale to measure them. For field work, identify complete spikelet units and count individual fertile florets, not all spikelets in the whole head.
tiles.short: Real green spikelets and yellow anthers — not a complete rooted plant
tiles.status: NINE GENUINE TEXAS BROME FIELD PHOTOS; FLOWERING SHOOT IN SOIL, REAL SPIKELETS, STILL NO EXPOSED ROOTS

tiles.heading: 02 · ANNUAL ROOTS AND ACTUAL COLLAR
tiles.details: The Texas Hill Country VEGETATIVE key (Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015) reports solitary or tufted annual shoots, pubescent nodes, rounded OPEN hairy sheaths, a continuous collar, and a 1–2-mm TRUNCATE EROSE membrane ligule. FNA describes a 2–3-mm lanceolate, pubescent, obtuse/erose ligule; WFO gives culm leaves 2–3(–3.5) mm and dorsal hairs, while Kew calls the margin eciliate. These differ partly by tissue/leaf position and treatment. New genuine Texas photos 7 (outer sheath) and 8 (true culm node) show the exterior. New source-verified New Braunfels panels 13 and 14 show the ACTUAL OPENED INNER blade/sheath junction with a translucent tissue flap consistent with membranous ligule and its side view. Because it may be partly torn and lacks a 1-mm ruler, free-edge identity and length are still not certified. Panel 12 shows the base above rocky soil, but NO exposed fibrous roots. These are real progress on the correct anatomy without pretending the annual root crown is photographed. Next: a source-verified flowering plant with intact fibrous base, one split sheath, blade/sheath INSIDE junction face-on and dorsal membrane beside physical 1-mm ruler. Never label a node or outer sheath hair as a ligule.
tiles.short: Actual open inside collar photographs now present; ligule 1-mm measurement and fibrous roots pending
tiles.status: REAL OUTER SHEATH, NODE AND INNER COLLAR MEMBRANE PHOTOGRAPHED; FREE LIGULE MM SCALE/ROOTS MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE TWO PERSISTENT GLUMES
tiles.details: Dissect ONE mature source-authenticated Texas-brome spikelet. Remove and backlight the TWO basal OUTER GLUMES — not inner lemma bracts — with a real millimeter ruler. FNA reports lower 6–9 mm/ONE vein, upper 8–10.5 mm/THREE veins; GrassBase lists somewhat shorter lengths but agrees on 1/3 venation. This excludes Japanese brome (often lower 3–5, upper 7) but does not alone prove TEXAS brome: other bromes such as B. tectorum ALSO can have 1/3-veined glumes. Panel 2 Japanese and panel 3 lanceolate are DIFFERENT species. New source-verified real Texas green spikelets in panels 9 and 10 are good for finding the floral bracts but DO NOT individually resolve lower or upper glume veins. The illustration is not photographic proof of 1/3 venation.
tiles.short: 1-veined lower / 3-veined upper glumes: critical but NOT unique
tiles.status: CRITICAL REAL BACKLIT SAME-VOUCHER GLUME PAIR NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA TIP AND SUBAPICAL AWN — HOLD CONFLICT
tiles.details: FNA/WFO describe an entire acute-to-subulate lemma tip, lemma 9–15 mm and a straight awn 4–8 mm inserted less than 1.5 mm below its apex. Kew GrassBase describes a short two-lobed or bifid apex and 6–10 mm awn. Do NOT blend these as if one photographic character is settled. In the single authentic Texas photo, whole projecting awns are visible but the lemma tip and awn insertion are not resolved; panel 1's ink drawing cannot establish the photographed specimen's apex. The next specimen should have both adaxial/dorsal 10–20× macro of a separated fully mature lemma with its end and original awn, physical 1-mm reference and confirmed voucher.
tiles.short: Lemma tip differences held: FNA entire, Kew bifid
tiles.status: LITERATURE TIP DISAGREEMENT RETAINED; ANATOMICALLY CERTAIN REAL LEMMA MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · LOOK-ALIKES — JAPANESE, LANCEOLATE, WOODLAND
tiles.details: Existing DIFFERENT-species panels: 2 = introduced B. japonicus, 3 = introduced B. lanceolatus, 4 = native perennial B. pubescens, and 5/6 = introduced broad-floreted rescuegrass B. catharticus. Panel 0 is the ONLY photographed B. texensis. Important additional look-alike: B. tectorum (not yet pictured in this gallery) may also have lower 1-veined and upper 3-veined glumes, but generally has longer awns and different leafy growth/sheath characters. The native Texas brome is scarce in regional floras; keep Bromus sp. if an observed plant lacks measured specimen evidence instead of automatically removing it or claiming native Hays presence from a generalized Texas distribution.
tiles.short: Compare actual Japanese panel 2, lanceolate panel 3, woodland panel 4
tiles.status: IDENTITIES AND LIMITS VERIFIED; NATIVE-VS-INTRODUCED COMPARISON NOT MORPHOLOGICALLY CLOSED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO LANE HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a source-vouchered rooted flowering Texas-brome annual with actual fibrous root crown and hairy lower sheaths, inner true membranous ligule with a physical 1-mm ruler, complete flowering head, mature opened single spikelet showing separately two BACKLIT glumes and actually counted veins, removed fertile lemma tip and subapical awn with mm scale. For hard look-alikes include verified B. tectorum and B. japonicus samples, because 1/3 venation alone is NOT diagnostic of Texas brome. NEEDS_SITE_QA: NINE installed exact-species CC BY Texas photographic JPEGs (one original Cleveland Powell, five additional Cleveland Powell, three Eric Knight New Braunfels), ONE PD historical illustration distinct from a real photo, five other-species comparison panels, original 15 markers kept, exact individual photo rights and displayed credits/mobile arrows, successful Pages deployment. Keep range flags and FNA vs Kew/WFO lemma-tip/ligule disagreements; don't mark 100%.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — nine real Texas images, key measured glumes and roots still missing
tiles.status: PHOTOS PUBLIC-READY FOR PROVISIONAL LEARNING; DIAGNOSTIC ROOT/GLUME/LEMMA MICROSCOPE HOLD AND PAGES QA

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: TEXAS BROME: native Texas annual with soft hairy sheaths/nodes, open panicle and 4–7-flowered narrow awned spikelets. SOURCE-IDENTIFIED flowering photo (gallery 0) shows actual yellow anthers and spikelets; it does NOT prove roots or collar. Before confusing with introduced Japanese/lanceolate or other Bromus, dissect mature LOWER 1-veined + UPPER 3-veined glumes and check lemma/awn, ligule, growth form and verified source. WARNING: the 1/3 glume pattern alone is NOT unique to this species (e.g., downy brome also shares it). Do not authorize removal based on flowerhead silhouette or one vein pair alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1 · TRUE PHOTO: photo/panel 0 is Cleveland Powell's flowering Bromus texensis source photo with narrow green multi-flowered spikelets and yellow anthers. Roots and true leaf collar are OFF FRAME.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The Texas Hill Country VEGETATIVE key (Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015) reports solitary or tufted annual shoots, pubescent nodes, rounded OPEN hairy sheaths, a continuous collar, and a 1–2-mm TRUNCATE EROSE membrane ligule. FNA describes a 2–3-mm lanceolate, pubescent, obtuse/erose ligule; WFO gives culm leaves 2–3(–3.5) mm and dorsal hairs, while Kew calls the margin eciliate. These differ partly by tissue/leaf position and treatment. New genuine Texas photos 7 (outer sheath) and 8 (true culm node) show the exterior. New source-verified New Braunfels panels 13 and 14 show the ACTUAL OPENED INNER blade/sheath junction with a translucent tissue flap consistent with membranous ligule and its side view. Because it may be partly torn and lacks a 1-mm ruler, free-edge identity and length are still not certified. Panel 12 shows the base above rocky soil, but NO exposed fibrous roots. These are real progress on the correct anatomy without pretending the annual root crown is photographed. Next: a source-verified flowering plant with intact fibrous base, one split sheath, blade/sheath INSIDE junction face-on and dorsal membrane beside physical 1-mm ruler. Never label a node or outer sheath hair as a ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Cleveland Powell's source-labelled Texas-brome photo (panel 0) shows several narrow MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets, projecting awnlike tips and emerging yellow anthers. The published 4–7 florets per spikelet have NOT been counted or measured from these unscaled pixels. The original photo crops out the plant base. New Texas source-verified panel 12 shows a flowering shoot growing in rocky soil, and panels 9–11 show attached flowering branches and green spikelets. Actual fibrous roots are still underground and no one image documents a continuous extracted root-to-head specimen. Panel 1 is a historically printed Hitchcock/Chase LINE DRAWING, not a second plant photograph. FNA describes a loose panicle 8–15 cm long and spikelets about 20–30 mm with 4–7 florets, but the photograph has no scale to measure them. For field work, identify complete spikelet units and count individual fertile florets, not all spikelets in the whole head.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

It is consistent with a membranous ligule, a much better anatomical view than an outer sheath alone; nevertheless the exact free edge, any tearing artifact, hair origins and 1–3 mm height are NOT established without a true ruler/section.

SOURCE-IDENTIFIED flowering photo (gallery 0) shows actual yellow anthers and spikelets; it does NOT prove roots or collar. Before confusing with introduced Japanese/lanceolate or other Bromus, dissect mature LOWER 1-veined + UPPER 3-veined glumes and check lemma/awn, ligule, growth form and verified source. memory_rule: JAPANESE: annual, flexuous awned head, higher glume veins. TEXAS: annual, lower ONE & upper THREE glume veins. LANCEOLATE: giant many-flowered spikelets. WOODLAND: perennial + hairy lemmas. RESCUE: broad flat short/no-awn units (comparison only).
safety_note: 2026-10-26 Lane 5: genuine Cleveland Powell flowering image pixels read from existing GitHub JPEG, historical drawing separately classed; 15 prior broad arrows and licensing retained. No separately documented true root crown, leaf ligule, glume veins, or mature lemma insertion. 1/3 glume vein count is shared with other Bromus; it is a diagnostic combination only with other traits. Three-source ligule length and lemma tip disagreements documented, not silently resolved. New local photographs 0, arrows 0, Pages deployment UNVERIFIED.
field_rule: For native versus introduced Bromus, the important structures are glume VEINS, actual lemma dimensions and awns, and an annual or perennial rooted crown—not the word 'brome' or a pretty nodding head.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
